clue.text: Wallop on the ear flattened rumoured evil genius

indicators.note: what is rumoured is only heard said, so the preceding words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: a wallop is a blow, and 'on the ear' asks only for how it sounds
knocked flat is felled

explanation.surface: A punch to the ear lays out the evil genius, so the gossip goes.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'blow felled' gives BLOFELD, the cat-stroking villain of the James Bond books and films.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernst Stavro Blofeld is the criminal mastermind who heads SPECTRE in Ian Fleming's Bond stories.

clue.text: Bowled wild, lousy bouncer — that'll do nicely!

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters run loose into a new order

blocks.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator: a wild delivery, a poor bouncer, and the batsman is out.
explanation.walkthrough: A bouncer is a short cricket ball that rears up at the batsman; 'bowled' supplies its scorecard B.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob's your uncle is a British idiom meaning 'and there you are, job done', just as 'that'll do nicely' signals satisfaction.

clue.text: Spinster game for a bit of fun!?

definitions.text: game for a bit of fun

blocks.note: first meaning: an older unmarried woman, an old-fashioned term

blocks.clueFragment: game for a bit of fun
blocks.note: second meaning: a light-hearted card game in which nobody wants the odd queen

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a single woman up for some mischief; the exclamation and question mark flag the cheeky reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated label for an unmarried woman and also the name of a simple children's card game.

clue.text: Order English dictionary (abridged version)

indicators.note: an abridged version is a shortened one, so the long word loses its ending

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone orders a shortened English dictionary.
explanation.walkthrough: DICT is the standard short form of dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official decree or proclamation, an order issued by an authority.

clue.text: Set off roughly at one, after Ted turns up

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading from bottom to top, so the name runs backwards
roughly means approximately or carelessly, so these letters come out in a loose order
after places the jumbled letters second, following the reversed name

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ted arrives and sets off at about one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the jumbled letters first, but 'after' sends them behind the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate a bomb is to make it explode, which is to set it off.

clue.text: Talk informally about vacant lease property

indicators.note: a vacant word is emptied of its insides, leaving just its two end letters
about means going round, so the informal talk wraps around what follows

blocks.note: a chat is informal talk
only the first and last letters of lease stay

explanation.surface: Someone chats casually about an empty rental property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lease property' looks like one phrase, but property alone is the definition and lease is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is a kind of house or holiday cabin, so it is a piece of real estate or property.

clue.text: Cover article featured in issue of newspaper

indicators.note: something featured in a publication appears inside it, so the article sits within

blocks.note: a single copy is one issue of a newspaper
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A cover story featured in today's edition of the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' and 'article' suggest journalism; article is the grammatical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A canopy is an overhead covering, such as fabric stretched above a bed or a tree's leafy roof.

clue.text: A haggard, grasping old New York columnist

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold tight, so the haggard word clutches what follows inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
gaunt means haggard and drawn
O is the abbreviation for old
NY is the abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: A worn-looking, money-grubbing veteran New York newspaper writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grasping' reads as greedy, but it means holding: G(ONY)AUNT after A.
explanation.definitionFit: An agony aunt writes a newspaper or magazine advice column answering readers' personal problems.

clue.text: Identify bear market stocks

indicators.note: a shop that stocks goods holds them, so the phrase holds the answer within it

blocks.note: spans letters 2-8 of 'bear market'

explanation.surface: Spotting which shares to pick in a falling stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocks' sounds like part of the finance picture, but it is the signal that holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To earmark something is to mark it out or designate it for a particular purpose, so to identify it.

clue.text: Sport club admin — tonight: boxing

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing, so the phrase before it holds the answer inside its letters

blocks.note: runs from the last letter of club through admin into the start of tonight

explanation.surface: A sports club's administrator announces that tonight's session is boxing.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxing looks like the sport being defined, but it is the signal; the sport sits inside clu(B ADMIN TON)ight.
explanation.definitionFit: Badminton is a racket game played over a net with a shuttlecock, so it is a sport.

clue.text: Four druids regularly pruned plant

indicators.note: pruning at regular intervals cuts away every other letter and keeps the rest

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A quartet of druids trimming a plant in a sacred grove.
explanation.definitionFit: Orris is a kind of iris whose root is used in perfumery, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Miss her chocolates terribly

indicators.note: terribly means very badly, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone pining terribly for her chocolates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb meaning to long for, but it is the title pupils give a female teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: British schoolchildren address a female teacher as 'Miss', so the title stands for the teacher herself.

clue.text: Raising agent, Smiley made Karla Circus target last of all

indicators.note: the last letter of every word in the run is the one to keep

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the five words

explanation.walkthrough: Smiley, Karla and the Circus come from John le Carré's spy novels; the names are only fodder here.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast makes bread dough rise, so bakers call it a raising agent.

clue.text: Irritation that might make one go completely potty?

definitions.text: Irritation that might make one go completely potty?

blocks.note: surface reading: something so annoying it drives you mad

blocks.clueFragment: Irritation that might make one go completely potty?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a skin soreness in an infant that might hurry along toilet training, when the child moves to the potty for good

explanation.walkthrough: Potty is British slang for crazy, and also a small child's toilet; the irritation is a baby's skin complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the red, sore skin a baby gets from a wet or soiled nappy, the British word for a diaper.

clue.text: Wave adult off after visiting one in Paris

indicators.note: something off has gone bad or is out of order, so the letters of the adult are jumbled
a visitor goes inside someone's home, so the jumbled word ends up inside the French word

blocks.note: the French feminine for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Waving an adult goodbye after a trip to Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled adult sits inside UNE, giving UN-DULAT-E.
explanation.definitionFit: To undulate is to move with a rolling, rippling motion, which is to wave as a verb.

clue.text: Civic dignitary upset royal when stealing gold coin from Germany

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the royal word's letters are tumbled
a thief takes things into their keeping, so the letters for gold and coin are taken inside

blocks.note: taken as written
or is the heraldic word for gold
DM is the Deutschmark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A mayor annoys the royals by pocketing a gold German coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lord Mayor is the ceremonial head of certain British cities, such as London, a civic dignitary.

clue.text: One clocked going round the bend?

blocks.note: first meaning: the little bird that pops out of a ... clock
second meaning: crazy, mad

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a speeding motorist caught on camera at a corner; 'clocked' means housed in a clock, and 'round the bend' is slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the mechanical bird of a cuckoo clock and is also informal slang for someone crazy.

clue.text: Army off icer, upper-class, embarrassed to be taken prisoner

blocks.note: Capt is the abbreviation for captain, an army officer
U is the British label for upper-class usage
an embarrassed person goes red

explanation.surface: A posh army captain blushes with shame at being taken prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The source prints 'officer' split as 'off icer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Captured means seized and held as a prisoner, the same as taken prisoner.

clue.text: Man in white uniform parking in boggy area

indicators.note: in tells us the parking letter is placed inside the word for a bog

blocks.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a mire is a stretch of swampy ground
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A man in a white uniform parks his car in a bog.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket umpires wear white coats, which is why the clue calls one a man in white; U then M(P)IRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket umpire traditionally stands in a long white coat, so he is the man in white on the field.

clue.text: Liquorice cake sent by favourite of Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner is the clergyman famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: sent by is from and a favourite is a pet; Spooner swaps their opening sounds

explanation.surface: A liquorice treat sent by Spooner's favourite pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From pet' with the opening sounds exchanged gives Pom-fret.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pomfret cake is a small round liquorice sweet originally made in Pontefract, Yorkshire.

clue.text: Authoritarian French painter tours Britain every now and again

to tour a place is to go all round it, so the painter's name surrounds the chosen letters

blocks.note: Édouard Manet, the French painter
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A strict French artist making an occasional trip round Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a stern disciplinarian who demands rigid obedience, which is an authoritarian person.

clue.text: North East German Krumm discovered patent medicine

the surname without its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'East German' reads as a nationality, but it asks for east in German.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack remedy of dubious effect, such as a patent medicine sold by its maker.

clue.text: Try, try right away to be enthusiastic

blocks.note: a judge will hear or try a case in court
taken as written

clue.text: Competitor of Cheshire Cat getting leg trapped

clue.text: Almost noon; leaving in good time

clue.text: Rather rocky 100sqm plot contained valuable oxide

explanation.definitionFit: Rare earths are oxides of the lanthanide metals, prized industrial materials, so a rare earth is a valuable oxide.

clue.text: Julius: boring, dull fantasist
